Description: anti-pattern — porting a Native font-faces config to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** Yes – the same `font-faces` block you use in a MapLibre Native style can be copied into a MapLibre GL JS style and will give you the same “offline-font” behaviour, **provided** the font files are reachable to the browser (i.e. served over HTTP/S or cached with a Service Worker). Below is a step-by-step checklist, the exact things that differ between the two SDKs, and a few gotchas to keep in mind. --- ## 1. What `font-faces` does in GL JS | Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS (≥ 6.7.0) | |---------|----------------|------------------------| | **Specification** | `root.font-faces` – maps a `text-font` name → one or more font files (TTF/OTF/WOFF) with optional `unicode-range`. | Same JSON property, read by the GL JS style parser. | | **Loading mechanism** | Reads the URL directly from the device’s file system or from a network URL (Android 11.13+, iOS 6.18+). | Loads the URL through the browser’s normal fetch pipeline (`` → `FontFace` API). | | **When it is used** | Always – even if a `glyphs` URL is present. | Always – **unless** you are in the “local-fonts only” mode (see §2) where the `glyphs` field is omitted and the browser’s CSS font-family resolution is used. | | **Shaping / complex scripts** | HarfBuzz (native) – works as soon as the font file is present. | Browser text engine (Chrome/Firefox/Safari) – works automatically once the font is loaded. | | **Offline** | You can ship the font files inside the app bundle. | You must make the files reachable via HTTP(S) **and** cache them (e.g. Service Worker, `Cache` API, or bundling them as data-URIs). | > **Bottom line:** The JSON syntax is identical, so you can copy the block verbatim. The only extra work is making sure the URLs are fetchable by the browser. --- ## 2. Two ways to get “offline-font” behaviour in GL JS ### A. **Keep a `glyphs` URL but add `font-faces`** (recommended if you still want fallback glyph PBFs for scripts that GL JS cannot render locally) ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://my-cdn.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "fonts/NotoSans-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] }, { "url": "fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": [ "U+3000-30FF", "U+3400-4DBF", "U+4E00-9FFF", "U+F900-FAFF", "U+FF00-FFEF" ] } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F"] } ] }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` *What happens* 1. **When the map needs a glyph** it first checks `font-faces`. 2. If the requested code point falls inside a declared `unicode-range`, the browser-loaded font is used (no PBF request). 3. If the code point is **outside** any declared range, the style falls back to the `glyphs` URL and fetches the appropriate PBF. This mirrors exactly what you already have in Native. ### B. **Omit the `glyphs` field entirely** – “pure-local-fonts” mode (GL JS ≥ 5.11.0) ```json { "version": 8, "font-faces": { … same as above … }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` *What happens* * The style is treated like a normal web page: every `text-font` name is resolved exactly as a CSS `font-family` list. * The browser loads the fonts you declared in `font-faces`. * No glyph-PBF requests are ever made, so the map works completely offline **as long as the font files are cached**. > **When to use this?** > *If you have *all* the fonts you need locally* (including CJK, Arabic, Devanagari, etc.) and you want to avoid any network traffic, this is the cleanest approach. > *If you still need a fallback for a script you haven’t packaged* (e.g. a rare historic script), keep a `glyphs` URL as in option A. --- ## 3. Making the font files reachable to the browser | Situation | What you need to do | |-----------|---------------------| | **Static hosting (e.g. CDN, GitHub Pages, your own web server)** | Place the `.woff2`/`.ttf` files under a public path (`/fonts/…`). The URLs in `font-faces` must be absolute or root-relative (`"/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.woff2"`). | | **Bundled with the app (e.g. Webpack, Vite, Create-React-App)** | Import the font as a module so the bundler emits a URL, then reference that URL in the style (or set it at runtime with `map.setFontFaces`). Example with Vite:
`import NotoSans from '/src/assets/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.woff2';`
`style.fontFaces = { "Noto Sans Regular": [{ url: NotoSans, "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"] }] };` | | **Pure offline (no network at all)** | Use a **Service Worker** to pre-cache the font files during the first load, or embed them as **data-URIs** (base64) directly in the `url` field. Data-URIs are large, but they guarantee zero network requests. | | **CORS** | The font files must be served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or the origin of your page). Otherwise the browser will block the `FontFace` load and fall back to the glyph server (or nothing). | --- ## 4. Runtime API – `map.setFontFaces()` If you need to **add or replace** fonts after the map has been created (e.g. you download a new font pack on-demand), you can call: ```javascript map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"] }, { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": [ "U+3000-30FF", "U+3400-4DBF", "U+4E00-9FFF", "U+F900-FAFF", "U+FF00-FFEF" ] } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.woff2", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"] } ] }); ``` *The call merges with any `font-faces` already present in the style.* This is handy for progressive-offline apps that first load a minimal Latin font and later download CJK or Arabic packs. --- ## 5. Special script notes for GL JS | Script | Do you need `font-faces`? | Anything extra? | |--------|--------------------------|-----------------| | **CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean)** | **No** if you keep the default `localIdeographFontFamily` (TinySDF). If you want a specific CJK font, declare it in `font-faces` **and** set `localIdeographFontFamily` to `false` **or** use a custom `text-font` name that points to your CJK file (see example in the skill). | | **Arabic / Hebrew** | From GL JS 6.9.0 onward, the browser shapes RTL text automatically; just provide the font via `font-faces`. No `setRTLTextPlugin` needed. | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | Since GL JS 6.15.0 the browser draws whole grapheme clusters, so the glyph server is ignored. Provide the script-specific font in `font-faces` with the appropriate `unicode-range`. | | **Mixed-script labels** (e.g., Latin + Arabic in the same string) | The first matching `unicode-range` wins per code-point. If you want Latin to stay in *Noto Sans* and Arabic in *Noto Sans Arabic*, list both fonts in the same `font-faces` block with disjoint ranges – the engine will switch automatically. | --- ## 6. Checklist before you ship 1. **Copy the `font-faces` block** from your Native style into the GL JS style (JSON or JS object). 2. **Verify URLs**: they must be reachable from the browser (CORS enabled). 3. **Decide on `glyphs`**: * Keep it if you want a fallback for any script you haven’t packaged. * Omit it if you truly want a fully offline map. 4. **Test offline**: * Open DevTools → Network → Offline. * All label layers should still render. If any disappear, check the console for “Failed to load font” errors. 5. **Cache the fonts** (Service Worker, `Cache` API, or embed as data-URIs) if you expect users to load the map without a network connection after the first visit. 6. **Optional – set `localIdeographFontFamily`** if you want to override the default CJK handling for layers that keep the default `text-font`. --- ## 7. Minimal working example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre GL JS – offline fonts

Description: explicit — right-to-left Arabic and Hebrew labels on GL JS 6
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS 6 map has Arabic and Hebrew place names. What do I need to set up so those labels read right-to-left with the Arabic letters joined correctly?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step checklist** that gets Arabic & Hebrew place-name labels rendering correctly on a MapLibre GL JS 6 map: | What you need | Why it matters | How to do it | |---------------|----------------|--------------| | **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.9.0** | Starting with 6.9.0 the library ships its own HarfBuzz-based shaping engine and RTL layout logic. The old `setRTLTextPlugin` is no longer required (and is deprecated). | Check the version you load (`maplibregl.version`). If it’s older, upgrade the script/npm package. | | **Unicode-correct text** | RTL shaping only works when the source string is in logical order (the normal Unicode order). | In your source data keep the Arabic/Hebrew names in their natural Unicode order (e.g. `"مكة"` not reversed). | | **A font that contains the script** | The on-device SDF glyph fallback can only draw Latin-ish characters. Arabic/Hebrew need a real font file so the browser can shape the glyphs. | Load a web-font (or use a system font) that covers the script – the easiest is the Noto family: `Noto Sans Arabic`, `Noto Sans Hebrew`. | | **Declare the font in the style (`font-faces`)** | `font-faces` tells both GL JS and Native which font file corresponds to the name you use in `text-font`. Without it the browser will fall back to whatever it finds on the system, which can be inconsistent across devices. | Add a `font-faces` block at the root of the style (or set it at runtime with `map.setFontFaces`). Example below. | | **Reference the font in `text-font`** | `text-font` is the cascade that the style uses for a label. Put the Arabic/Hebrew font first, then a generic fallback. | `"text-font": ["Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "Noto Sans Regular", "sans-serif"]` (Hebrew uses `"Noto Sans Hebrew Regular"`). | | **(Optional) `glyphs` URL** | You can keep a `glyphs` URL for Latin/other scripts – it will be ignored for Arabic/Hebrew because the browser does the shaping. | No change needed; just make sure the URL points at a working glyph server for the other fonts you use. | | **(Optional) `localIdeographFontFamily`** | This option only affects CJK ideographs, **not** Arabic/Hebrew, so you can leave it at the default. | No action required. | --- ## 1️⃣ Verify you are on GL JS 6.9.0 or newer ```html ``` ```js console.log('MapLibre version →', maplibregl.version); // should be ≥ 6.9.0 ``` If you are still on 6.8.x or older, upgrade – the RTL shaping code lives in the core library now. --- ## 2️⃣ Load the required font files You can host the fonts yourself or pull them from a CDN. **Example using the Google-hosted Noto fonts (CORS-enabled):** ```html ``` Or, if you prefer to bundle them: ```text /public/fonts/ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf ``` Make sure the URLs you expose are reachable from the page (CORS headers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your own domain). --- ## 3️⃣ Declare the fonts in the style (`font-faces`) Add a `font-faces` object at the **root** of your style JSON (or set it later with `map.setFontFaces`). Only the `unicode-range` that covers the script is needed; everything else will fall back to the glyph server. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }, "layers": [ /* … your layers … */ ] } ``` **Runtime alternative** (if you cannot edit the style file): ```js map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }); ``` > **Tip:** The `unicode-range` entries are optional – you can omit them and the whole file will be used for any codepoint. Adding the ranges just makes the engine skip the file for unrelated characters, which can be a tiny performance win. --- ## 4️⃣ Use the font in your label layers ```json { "id": "place-labels-arabic", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"], "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name_ar"], // Arabic name column "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", // first choice – will be used for Arabic shaping "Noto Sans Regular", // fallback for Latin parts (e.g. numbers) "sans-serif" ], "text-size": 12, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` For Hebrew you would duplicate the layer (or add a separate filter) and use `"text-field": ["get", "name_he"]` with `"text-font": ["Noto Sans Hebrew Regular", "Noto Sans Regular", "sans-serif"]`. **Important:** Do **not** set `text-direction` – MapLibre automatically detects RTL direction from the Unicode bidirectional algorithm. The only thing you need to ensure is that the string you feed is in logical order (the normal order you store in the database). --- ## 5️⃣ (If you ever need the old plugin) – legacy note If you are stuck on a pre-6.9.0 version for some reason, you must load the RTL text plugin **once**, *before* creating the map: ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/@mapbox/mapbox-gl-rtl-text@0.3.0/dist/mapbox-gl-rtl-text.js', false // false = do not wait for the plugin to load before creating the map ); ``` After that the rest of the steps (font-faces, `text-font`) are the same. But upgrading is strongly recommended – the plugin is deprecated and will be removed in a future major release. --- ## 6️⃣ Quick sanity-check checklist | ✅ | Item | |---|------| | **Version** | `maplibregl.version >= 6.9.0` | | **Font files** | Accessible URLs (CORS enabled) for Arabic & Hebrew fonts | | **`font-faces`** | Declared in the style (or via `map.setFontFaces`) with the same names you use in `text-font` | | **`text-font`** | Arabic/Hebrew font name appears first in the cascade | | **Data** | Arabic/Hebrew names stored in logical Unicode order (`name_ar`, `name_he`) | | **`glyphs`** | Still present for Latin/other scripts (optional) – does not affect Arabic/Hebrew | | **No RTL plugin** | Not needed for GL JS ≥ 6.9.0 | If you follow the checklist, Arabic and Hebrew place-name labels will: * be laid out right-to-left automatically, * have proper contextual shaping (joined letters, ligatures, diacritics), * look the same across browsers because the same font file is used, and * fall back gracefully to the glyph server for any Latin characters that appear in the same label (e.g., numbers). --- ### TL;DR Code snippet (full minimal example) ```html Arabic & Hebrew RTL labels
``` Replace `https://example.com/fonts/...` with the real URLs where you host the TTF/OTF files. Once the map loads, Arabic and Hebrew place names will appear correctly shaped and right-to-left. Happy mapping!

Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR 1. **Upgrade MapLibre GL JS** to **≥ 6.15.0** (or at least ≥ 6.7.0). 2. **Declare the Devanagari font in `font-faces`** (or load it as a web-font) and give it a proper `unicode-range`. 3. Keep the `glyphs` URL **or omit it** – it no longer matters for Devanagari once the font-face is declared. 4. Use the exact **`text-font` name** that you declared in `font-faces`. 5. (Optional) Call `map.setFontFaces()` at runtime if you need to change the mapping after the map is created. After those steps the vowel signs, matras and conjuncts will be shaped correctly. --- ## Why the problem happens | What you have | What MapLibre did (pre-6.7) | |---------------|-----------------------------| | `glyphs` URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari PBFs | Each Unicode code-point was fetched from the PBF and drawn **individually**. The glyph server cannot provide the complex shaping required for Devanagari (conjuncts, vowel signs, reordering). The result is “letters on top of each other” or misplaced matras. | | GL JS ≥ 6.7 | The engine switched to **grapheme-cluster rendering** using the browser’s text layout engine (HarfBuzz-style shaping). The glyph PBFs are ignored for scripts that need shaping; the browser-provided font is used instead. | | GL JS ≥ 6.15 | The shaping is now **always** used for Devanagari, even when a `glyphs` URL is present, and the `font-faces` property is honoured for picking the exact font file. | So the fix is simply to **use a recent MapLibre version** and **tell the map which font file to use** via `font-faces`. --- ## Step-by-step fix ### 1. Upgrade to a recent MapLibre GL JS version ```bash # npm / yarn npm install maplibre-gl@^6.15.0 # or the latest 6.x release # or use a CDN tag that points to ≥6.15.0 ``` > **Why ≥ 6.15?** > * 6.7 introduced grapheme-cluster rendering for complex scripts. > * 6.9 added proper Arabic shaping (irrelevant here but good to have). > * 6.15 made the behavior **consistent**: the glyph server is bypassed for Devanagari and the `font-faces` mapping is always respected. If you cannot upgrade (e.g. locked to an older version), the only workaround is to **remove the `glyphs` URL** and rely on the *local-fonts* fallback introduced in GL JS 5.11, but that still requires a recent version to get proper shaping. ### 2. Add a `font-faces` entry for Devanagari The style’s root object gets a `font-faces` property. It maps the **exact `text-font` name** you will use in your layers to one (or more) font files, optionally limited to a Unicode range. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // can stay, or be omitted "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] // Devanagari block } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels-hi", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"], "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"], // Hindi name tag "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], // fallback "text-size": 12 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` **Key points** * **`text-font` name** (`"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"` in the example) **must match the key** in `font-faces`. * The `unicode-range` tells MapLibre to use this file **only for Devanagari code points**; everything else falls back to the next font in the list (or to the glyph server if you kept it). * The URL must be reachable from the browser (CORS-enabled, HTTPS, etc.). ### 3. (Optional) Load the font-face at runtime If you need to add or replace a font after the map is already created, call `map.setFontFaces()`: ```javascript const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'style.json', center: [77.2, 28.6], zoom: 10 }); map.on('style.load', () => { map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }); }); ``` ### 4. Verify the result * Open the map, zoom in on Hindi labels. * The vowel signs (matras) should now sit **above, below, or to the side** of the base consonant as expected, and conjuncts (e.g. “क्ष”, “त्र”) should appear as a single glyph. * Open the browser dev-tools → **Network** tab and confirm **no `.pbf` requests** are made for Devanagari code points (they are rendered locally). If you still see broken shaping: | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | Letters still drawn individually | Still using a pre-6.7 version | Upgrade to ≥ 6.7 (preferably ≥ 6.15). | | No font applied (fallback to generic sans-serif) | `text-font` name does not match `font-faces` key, or the URL is blocked by CORS. | Ensure exact name match and that the font file is CORS-enabled (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your domain). | | Glyphs from the server are still requested | `font-faces` entry missing `unicode-range` or range does not cover the code points. | Add the correct `unicode-range` (`U+0900-097F`). | | Map crashes or shows “Unable to load glyph range …” | `glyphs` URL points to a non-existent server. | Either fix the URL or **remove the `glyphs` field** entirely (local-fonts mode). | --- ## Full minimal example (HTML) ```html Hindi labels – correct Devanagari shaping
``` Replace `https://example.com/fonts/...` with the real URL where you host the Devanagari TTF/OTF (or a CDN copy). --- ## What about the `glyphs` URL? * **You can keep it** – it will still be used for scripts that *do* need glyph PBFs (e.g. Latin, Arabic, CJK if you explicitly disable `localIdeographFontFamily`). * **You can remove it** – if you only need Devanagari (or any script that is now rendered locally) you can omit the field entirely and rely on the local-fonts fallback introduced in GL JS 5.11. This makes the style completely offline-friendly (as long as the web-fonts are reachable). --- ## Summary checklist | ✅ | Action | |---|--------| | **Upgrade** | Use MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.15.0 (or at least 6.7). | | **Declare font-face** | Add a `font-faces` entry for the Devanagari font with a proper `unicode-range`. | | **Match names** | Ensure `text-font` in your symbol layers exactly matches the key in `font-faces`. | | **CORS** | Verify the font file can be fetched by the browser (CORS headers). | | **Test** | No `.pbf` requests for Devanagari; labels look correct. | | **Optional** | Remove the `glyphs` field if you want a pure local-font setup. | After completing those steps, Hindi labels will be rendered with proper vowel-sign placement and conjunct formation, just like native text editors. Happy mapping!
